planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring and pot into a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, keeping newly divided plants on the dry side until roots establish.

directions: This small Eastern Cape succulent forms an upright column of thick, triangular, tightly overlapping leaves arranged in neat vertical rows, a growth habit distinctive enough to once earn it its own genus, Poellnitzia, before taxonomists folded it into Astroloba. In spring its wiry flower stalks carry an unusual feature among Haworthia relatives: tubular, bright coral-red flowers rather than the dull cream or greenish blooms typical of its kin. Grow in bright filtered light or morning sun with shade from the hottest afternoon exposure, in a mineral-rich, fast-draining succulent mix, and allow the soil to dry fully between waterings. It slowly offsets at the base to form small clustering groups and is most easily propagated by removing and potting these rooted offsets.

planting.note: Plant the bulb with its neck at the soil surface at the start of the autumn rains so the leaf pair and flower spike develop through the cool winter growing season.

directions: Whiteheadia bifolia produces just two broad, ground-hugging leaves with distinctly wavy margins that lie flat against the soil, while a dense, cylindrical flower spike rises between them, wrapped in persistent, downward-reflexed greenish bracts that give the inflorescence a shaggy, tiered appearance. Small greenish-white flowers open in succession up the spike in late winter and spring. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining mix and water through the cool rainy season, then withhold water completely once the leaves yellow and die back for its dry summer dormancy. Native to sandy flats in South Africa's Western Cape, it is a slow-multiplying specialist bulb usually increased from offsets.

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly in spring just as summer rains begin so the grass-like leaves and flowering stem can develop through the warm growing season.

directions: Dipcadi viride is a small, wiry-stemmed bulb widespread across summer-rainfall regions of South Africa and tropical Africa, producing a loose tuft of narrow, grass-like basal leaves. Its slender flowering stem carries a one-sided raceme of small, drooping, bell-shaped flowers in muted shades of greenish-brown to olive, a subdued coloring that sets it apart from the showier bulbs it often grows alongside. Plant bulbs shallowly in free-draining, humus-poor soil and water regularly through the warm growing season, then keep nearly dry through its dormant winter rest. It remains a minor but genuine item among specialist African bulb collectors, propagated chiefly from offsets or seed.
